Claims 1-8 and 21-23 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 101 for being directed to non-statutory subject matter. Applicant respectfully traverses this rejection and requests that it be withdrawn, for at least the following reasons.
The current test to determine whether a claim is directed toward patent eligible subject matter is the analysis based upon Alice Corp. Pty. Ltd. v. CLS Bank Int'l., 134 S. Ct. 2347

(2014) (hereinafter "Alice") and Mayo Collaborative Services v. Prometheus Laboratories, Inc., 132 S. Ct. 1289 (2011) (hereinafter "Mayo"). This test is essentially in two parts. "Supreme Court precedent instructs us to 'first determine whether the claims at issue are directed to a patent-ineligible concept."' Enfish, LLC v. Microsoft Corp., No. 2015-2044, slip op. at *9 (Fed. Cir. May 12, 2016) (quoting Alice, at 2347) (hereinafter "Enfish").
As "[t]he Supreme Court has not established a definitive rule to determine what

constitutes as an 'abstract idea' sufficient to satisfy the first step of the Mayo/Alice inquiry," the Court has "found it sufficient to compare claims at issue to those claims already found to be directed to an abstract idea in previous cases." Id. (citing Alice). "If this threshold determination is met, we move to the second step of the inquiry and 'consider the elements of each claim both individually and "as an ordered combination" to determine whether the additional elements "transform the nature of the claim" into a patent-eligible application."' Id. (quoting Alice (quoting Mayo)).
The analysis of the claims at issue will be presented below, discussing the claims in Parts 1, 2A and 2B.
Step 1 - Determine whether the claim is directed to one of the statutory categories of invention.
Step 2A - If the claim is directed to one of the statutory categories of invention, determine if the claim is, as a whole, directed to a judicial exception.

Step 2B - If the claim is, as a whole, directed to a judicial exception, analyze the claim elements, both individually and as a whole, to determine if there are additional limitations that amount to significantly more than the abstract idea.

As explained below, the claims satisfy Part 1 as they are directed to at least one of the statutory categories of invention, as well as Part 2A, as the claims are not directed to a judicially recognized exception. While analysis under Part 2B should not be required, the claims also satisfy the significantly more than an abstract idea test for a number of reasons, including the fact that the claims are specifically limited to a specific technical field. For these reasons, as discussed below, the claims are directed to patent-eligible subject matter.
Step 1: The claims are directed to one of the statutory categories of invention.
Applicant agrees with the Examiner that all of the claims meet the requirements of step
Step 2A: Prong One - Evaluate Whether the Claim Recites a Judicial Exception
The Office Action asserts that the claims recite an abstract idea that falls into the "Mental Processes" groupings. See Office Action p. 7. Applicant respectfully disagrees.

Initially, Applicant submits that the claims are not directed toward mental processes. The October 2019 Update to the Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility ("October 2019 Update") states that "[c]laims do not recite a mental process when they do not contain limitations that can practically be performed in the human mind." See October 2019 Update p. 2 (Notice provided at 84 Fed. Reg. 55942 (Oct. 18, 2019); substance of the Update published at https://www.uspto.gov) (emphasis added). Claim 1 recites, inter alia, a robotic arm positionable in any pose and configured to support an object, registering a patient to a pre- operative image to enable the robotic arm to be precisely positionable relative to the anatomical element, and reregistering the patient to the pre-operative image based on the notification indicating that the relative pose of the first tracking device and the second tracking device has changed, wherein reregistration of the patient enables the robotic arm to be precisely positionable relative to the anatomical element after the relative pose has changed. Applicant respectfully submits that such actions cannot be practically performed in the human mind. For example, the registration process and the reregistration process enables a robotic arm to be precisely positionable relative to an anatomical element, an action that cannot be practically performed in the human mind. Accordingly, the claims are not directed toward mental processes.
Since the pending claims are not directed toward an abstract idea, the pending claims are patent eligible. Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration and withdrawal of the rejection.
Step 2A: Prong Two - Evaluate Whether the Claim, As a Whole, Integrates the Recited Judicial Exception into a Practical Application of the Exception
Although Applicant believes the claims are not directed toward a judicial exception,
and that further analysis under Step 2A, Prong Two is believed to be redundant, the claims are
directed toward a practical application for at least the reason that they integrate the alleged judicial exception into a practical application.

The October 2019 Update indicates that "[in order to determine whether the claimed invention improves the functioning of a computer or other technology], first the specification should be evaluated to determine if the disclosure provides sufficient details such that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement. The specification need not explicitly set forth the improvement, but it must describe the invention such that the improvement would be apparent to one of ordinary skill in the art." Id. at 12. Then, "the claim must be evaluated to ensure that the claim itself reflect the disclosed improvement." Id. at 12.

The use of these technical solutions help ensure proper registration and/or reregistration during the surgical operation such that the robotic arm can be precisely positioned relative to the patient even after patient movement. Applicant submits that a person of ordinary skill in the art would, when viewing such a detailed disclosure, recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement.

Moreover, such technical solutions are recited by the claims. Indeed, independent claim 1 recites , a robotic arm positionable in any pose and configured to support an object, registering a patient to a pre-operative image to enable the robotic arm to be precisely positionable relative to the anatomical element, and reregistering the patient to the pre-operative image based on the notification indicating that the relative pose of the first tracking device and the second tracking device has changed, wherein reregistration of the patient enables the robotic arm to be precisely positionable relative to the anatomical element after the relative pose has changed. Applicant submits that these claim features recite the disclosed improvement to ensuring an accurate registration. Accordingly, the claim as a whole integrates the alleged judicial exception into a practical application.
Step 2B

Although Applicant submits that the currently pending claims are patent eligible under a Step 2A analysis as discussed above, Applicant also submits that the claims recite additional hardware elements that are sufficient to amount to "significantly more" than an abstract idea. For example, by affixing a first tracking device to a table and a second tracking device to an anatomical element having a pose relative to the table, patient movement relative to the table can be monitored. If patient movement is detected, then reregistration may occur so as to enable a robotic arm to be precisely positionable relative to the patient before and after patient movement. Thus, the claims amount to "significantly more" than an abstract idea.

For at least the foregoing reasons, Applicant respectfully submits that the second prong of the eligibility test properly results in a determination of patent-eligibility, and respectfully requests that the rejection of claims 1-8 under 35 U.S.C. § 101 be withdrawn.

Claims 1, 2, 7, 8, and 21-23 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being obvious over International Patent Publication No. 2020/072335 to Nikou et al. ("Nikou") in view of U.S. Publication No. 2019/0321657 to Hale ("Hale"). Claims 3-5 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being obvious over Nikou in view of Hale, and further in view of U.S. Patent Publication No. 2014/0206990 to Epstein et al. ("Epstein"). Claim 6 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being
obvious over Nikou in view of Hale in view of U.S. Patent Publication No. 2019/0090955 to Singh et al. ("Singh").

Claims 1 and 21 now recite, inter alia, a robotic arm positionable in any pose and configured to support an object, registering a patient to a pre-operative image to enable the robotic arm to be precisely positionable relative to the anatomical element, and reregistering the patient to the pre-operative image based on the notification indicating that the relative pose of the first tracking device and the second tracking device has changed, wherein reregistration of the patient enables the robotic arm to be precisely positionable relative to the anatomical element after the relative pose has changed.. None of the cited references taken together or separately appear to disclose, teach, or suggest the features recited in the amended claims.
Nikou teaches a system for performing a computer-aided surgical procedure in which

optical sensors detect and record the location of one or more optical tracking devices mounted to a patient. Nikou, Abstract. Nikou, however, does not teach a robotic arm positionable in any pose and configured to support an object, registering a patient to a pre-operative image to enable the robotic arm to be precisely positionable relative to the anatomical element, and reregistering the patient to the pre-operative image based on the notification indicating that the relative pose of the first tracking device and the second tracking device has changed, wherein reregistration of the patient enables the robotic arm to be precisely positionable relative to the anatomical element after the relative pose has changed. as recited in claims 1 and 21. Thus, Nikou does not disclose or teach the claimed limitations of claims 1 and 21.
Hale does not cure the deficiencies of Nikou. Hale teaches generating a model of a

portion of a patient based on images received from a stereo camera and comparing the model to a stored model of the portion of the patient to determine if the patent has moved. Hale, para. [0016]. Hale, however, does not teach a robotic arm positionable in any pose and configured to support an object, registering a patient to a pre-operative image to enable the robotic arm to be precisely positionable relative to the anatomical element, and reregistering the patient to the pre- operative image based on the notification indicating that the relative pose of the first tracking device and the second tracking device has changed, wherein reregistration of the patient enables the robotic arm to be precisely positionable relative to the anatomical element after the relative pose has changed. as recited in claims 1 and 21. Thus, Hale does not disclose or teach the claimed limitations of claims 1 and 21.

Epstein does not cure the deficiencies of Nikou or Hale. Epstein teaches a method for verifying a spatial registration of an anatomical region by tracking a spatial pose of at least one checkpoint defined within the anatomical region and tracking a spatial pose of a probe tip in proximity to the anatomical region at the checkpoint. Epstein, Abstract. Epstein, however, does not teach a robotic arm positionable in any pose and configured to support an object, registering a patient to a pre-operative image to enable the robotic arm to be precisely positionable relative to the anatomical element, and reregistering the patient to the pre-operative image based on the notification indicating that the relative pose of the first tracking device and the second tracking device has changed, wherein reregistration of the patient enables the robotic arm to be precisely positionable relative to the anatomical element after the relative pose has changed as recited in claim 1. Thus, Epstein does not disclose or teach the claimed limitations of claims 1 and 21.
Singh does not cure the deficiencies of Nikou or Hale. Singh teaches systems and

methods for estimating a pose of an anatomy and a pose of a surgical instrument relative to the anatomy by receiving visual and sensory information indicative of pose of the anatomy and surgical instruments relative to the anatomy. Singh, Abstract. Singh, however, does not teach a robotic arm positionable in any pose and configured to support an object, registering a patient to a pre-operative image to enable the robotic arm to be precisely positionable relative to the anatomical element, and reregistering the patient to the pre-operative image based on the notification indicating that the relative pose of the first tracking device and the second tracking device has changed, wherein reregistration of the patient enables the robotic arm to be precisely positionable relative to the anatomical element after the relative pose has changed as recited in claims 1 and 21. Thus, Singh does not disclose or teach the claimed limitations of claims 1 and 21.
Accordingly, the combination of Nikou, Hale, Epstein, and/or Singh fails to disclose
every limitation of claims 1-4, 6-8, and 21-23, and for at least this reason, Applicant respectfully requests that the rejection of claims 1-8 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 be withdrawn.
